Hi all, FusionCache creator here: let me know if you need anything.

Just FYI: `MemoryCache` does **not** have [cache stampede](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/CacheStampede.md) protection.

Also, after months of work, FusionCache V2 is about to be released in the next few weeks with a lot of extra features.

Here is the [last preview](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/releases/tag/v2.0.0-preview-4).

Hope this helps!

I don't know that much about Godot, so take this with a pinch of salt, but: for something so core and so core and so low level I would probably not use FusionCache, nor MemoryCache (its API surface area is not really great) nor anything like that at all.

I think I'd create something uber low level and 100% specialized for this exact purpose, basically something like a `Dictionary`/`ConcurrentDictionary` + massive use of `ReadOnlySpan<T>` or similar + some form of low level locking, if needed at all: for example if an extra string allocation in the worst case scenario is not the end of the world I may not even put a locking mechanism and just go with the native dictionary `GetOrAdd` method.

To be clear: I'm saying this not because FusionCache is bad, I mean, I created it (and FWIW I think it's really good 😬).

The thing is that it does **a lot** like [L1+L2](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/CacheLevels.md), [backplane](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/Backplane.md), [fail-safe](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/FailSafe.md), [eager-refresh](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/EagerRefresh.md), [conditional refresh](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/ConditionalRefresh.md), [auto-recovery](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/AutoRecovery.md) and way more, and if what is needed here is "just" an in-memory dictionary with some concurrent access mechanism, that may be overkill.

Hope this helps.

Hi @Joy-less 

> * It has to allocate a delegate for the factory function.

I'm not sure I got this 100% right, but to be clear: FusionCache can of course work with a static delegate and no allocation at all.
To be more explicit, I have created some benchmarks to test exactly this with a so called "read happy path", and the memory allocated is exactly zero bytes.

Hope this helps.

I removed the `WithCapacity(1_000)` because I thought it's too much of a magic number in comparison to `WithExpireAfterAccess(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))`, and I made the package private so it's not visible to Godot projects.
Is there a solid reason why we should invalidate the caches by time?

> Is there a solid reason why we should invalidate the caches by time?
@Delsin-Yu

The caches must be invalidated at some point to prevent Ruby's [symbols denial-of-service](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/24066556/getting-warning-denial-of-service) problem (at least before mortal symbols were introduced).
As for the method of invalidation, time-based is the best solution I could find. Note that it invalidates 30s after the last access not after caching. The PR mainly prevents situations where you're creating a new StringName or NodePath every frame; if it's not used for 30s then it won't impact performance to expunge it from the cache. Ideally, it would take into account the amount of available memory, but there doesn't seem to be a good way to do this. I think the approach I suggested works for 99.99% of cases and is easy to workaround if someone wants to use their own caching system.

> if it's not used for 30s then it won't impact performance to expunge it from the cache.

It almost sounds like your solution aims to address the use case where the engine user suddenly creates an unreasonable number of StringNames (or NodePaths). Is this common in a typical project?

> The PR mainly prevents situations where you're creating a new StringName or NodePath every frame;

Generally, the tiered GC (as opposed to the Unity's legacy non-moving non-tiered GC) can take care of a small number (<500? benchmark needed) of these creations (or not to create stuttering), as tier 0 object GC is generally very fast.

> It almost sounds like your solution aims to address the use case where the engine user suddenly creates an unreasonable number of StringNames (or NodePaths). Is this common in a typical project?

Very common, any project which uses them for getting nodes, checking input actions, setting shader parameters, or using GDScript variables will benefit from this.

> Generally, the tiered GC (as opposed to the Unity's legacy non-moving non-tiered GC) can take care of a small number (<500? benchmark needed) of these creations (or not to create stuttering), as tier 0 object GC is generally very fast.

Yes, C# is performant, but that doesn't mean it makes sense to make hidden allocations every frame for no reason.
I'm curious how the performance would be if you used a lower number instead of 200,000 in previous benchmarks.

> that doesn't mean it makes sense to make hidden allocations every frame for no reason.

I believe we need to first prove the performance issue exists before addressing them, `200_000` is not a fair number for benchmarking.

> to make hidden allocations every frame for no reason.

The documentation [did tell you](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/c_sharp/c_sharp_basics.html#current-gotchas-and-known-issues) to use the cached StringNames.

I believe caching can bring enough performance improvement, but I wonder if it's possible to implement a more fundamental solution to reduce the overhead of implicit conversion.
Compared with the implicit conversion of `StringName` in GDScript, how much slower it is in C#?

> I believe caching can bring enough performance improvement, but I wonder if it's possible to implement a more fundamental solution to reduce the overhead of implicit conversion.
> Compared with the implicit conversion of `StringName` in GDScript, how much slower it is in C#?

In GDScript it's not as big of a problem for three reasons:
1. StringNames/NodePaths are built into the language, so you have `&StringName` and `^NodePath` syntax and also the parser can detect implicit casts.
2. GDScript uses reference counting which results in slower performance but not garbage collection spikes. (I think)
3. GDScript is closer to C++ so it only has to maintain one StringName (rather than marshalling a C# copy)

@beicause Nice work! One possible problem with weak reference caching is that, if the garbage collector runs often, then string names / node paths could be collected and reallocated more often than they should. I think it could still be more ideal though since it will take into account the available memory of the system.

@beicause I replaced the `BitFaster.Caching` dependency with weak reference caching like you suggested. I made some changes to your implementation:
1. Your use of `TryGetValue` and `[]=` is not thread-safe. I changed it to `GetOrAdd`.
2. I noticed you added allocation-free conversions to `string` which is good. I made it so if it has to take the allocation path when converting to a string, it sets the cached string so it doesn't have to do it again.
3. I moved the cache cleanup from the finalizer to `Dispose`, so that disposed `StringName`/`NodePath`s are not fetched from the cache.

Note that the `NodePath.ToString`  should not return the original string. The result may be different from the original one after NodePath parses the string 

In addition, the explicitly constructed  StringName will also release the cache when it is disposed.

I'm not a expert, can we cache the  NativeValue when constructing the StringName?
 (This requires testing and might be a bottleneck, If this is the main bottleneck, we can even choose not to cache the  StringName itself)

I remade this pull request in a way that makes `StringName` and `NodePath` classes immutable, predictable, and thread-safe.

Here's how it works:
- Constructing a C# StringName or NodePath:
  - The constructor stores the input string in a private field (`_inputString`). This corresponds to the key in the cache.
  - The constructor stores the output string in a private field (`_outputString`). This string is calculated using the native value, or taken directly from the input string for StringNames since they can't be simplified.
- Converting a C# StringName or NodePath to a C# string:
  - The output string stored in `_outputString` is returned.
- Implicitly converting to a C# StringName or NodePath from a C# string:
  - There is an attempt to fetch an existing StringName or NodePath from the cache, using the input string as a key.
  - If not found, a new StringName or NodePath is created and returned. There is also an attempt to add it to the cache (which is ignored if this has already happened by another thread due to a race).
- Finalizing/disposing a C# StringName or NodePath:
  - The cache entry is removed if there is a cache entry matching the input string to the object being disposed.
- Comparing the equality of a C# StringName or NodePath and a C# string:
  - A new method (`Equals(string?)`) has been added. For StringNames, it compares the given string and `_outputString`. For NodePaths, it converts the given string to a native NodePath, compares the native handles, and disposes the new native NodePath (this should still avoid C# garbage collection).

The result:
- The fields of C# StringNames and NodePaths are readonly, making them immutable and therefore thread-safe.
- Converting StringNames and NodePaths to C# strings (e.g. through `.ToString()`) is free.
- Converting strings to StringNames and NodePaths via implicit conversion uses caching and therefore cheap.

~~One question:~~
~~- In the C# NodePath constructor that accepts a string, is it necessary to convert to/from a native handle to get the stringified version? In other words, is `new NodePath(from).ToString() == from` ever `false`?~~
Answer: yes it is, because `//` simplifies to `/`.
